posts.title: YE JIN
posts.text: I am currently a master’s student in Materials Science at TUM with a background in software development. I aim to contribute to the development of complete cures for neurological disorders such as Parkinson’s disease and Alzheimer’s. My research interests include micro/nano-biorobotics and brain modeling, driven by a strong passion for pioneering fundamental therapeutic strategies for brain diseases, supported by my solid foundation in materials science.

posts.title: From Microbots to YOLOv11 - My Internship Journey in Cell Culture & Microgel Counting
posts.text: I started my master’s because I want to contribute to the cure of neurodegenerative diseases like Parkinson’s and Alzheimer’s, and I’m planning to apply for a PhD in this field as well. I’m especially fascinated by micro/nano-biorobotics and brain tissue or neural modeling as tools for fundamental brain treatment. That’s why I joined the MBRL lab as an intern - to gain hands-on experience with cell culture and to learn how nanorobots can actually be built. At first, I was more interested in nanoparticles, but while writing my research proposal here, I realized how broad the field of microrobotics actually is: Design Actuation Locomotion Planning Tracking Navigation After analyzing four papers recommended by my professor, I found myself most drawn to Design and Navigation. Eventually, I wrote a proposal focused on “Dopamine-Responsive Aptamer Nanorobots for On-Demand and Targeted Levodopa Delivery in Parkinson’s Disease.” Through this process, I became particularly interested in working with BBB (blood-brain barrier) and CMOS-based microrobots. For example, I’m convinced that within the next decade, microrobots will inevitably evolve into self-controlled systems with built-in CMOS. And with continuous in vivo experiments, I also believe that there will be ways to bypass the BBB’s tight junctions and deliver drugs exactly where they’re needed. Alongside the proposal and learning cell culture (including passaging), I was given a very practical task - something that could actually contribute to the PhD students’ projects in the lab: Count the number of microgels and cells in these images. After refining the task with my supervising PhD student, the rules were set: Overlapping microgels and the cells inside them are not counted. Microgels cut off at the image edge with more than 50% outside are excluded. Cells are counted even if they overlap. Cells outside of any microgel are not counted. The output should be a single Excel file (.xlsx) with two sheets: microgel_id_cell_count – microgel ID and number of cells inside microgel_id_cell_id – microgel ID (duplicates allowed) and IDs of cells inside each microgel Since I had already taken AI classes, my first instinct was: wouldn’t segmentation be more accurate? Especially since there’s already a famous tool called CellPose. And indeed, using CellPose I was able to detect microgels… but then the problems started: The pre-trained model was hard to customize. Performance varied a lot by image - sometimes great, sometimes useless. With images full of microgels, it took over 5 minutes per image. (As a Korean, this was unacceptable, way too slow 😂) Cells inside microgels were barely detected. I even tried a naive approach — count “round” shapes inside microgels - but cells aren’t perfect circles, and overlaps broke the method completely. I also considered cropping each microgel into a separate image and then running CellPose… but just counting the microgels already overloaded the server. I literally had to rotate through 4–5 Google accounts just to keep using TPUs. → Segmentation was out. So I turned to YOLOv11 and object detection. Problem: no dataset. Solution: make one. I hand-labeled 49 images. It took me 8 hours straight Haha The model trained, but of course, with only 49 images, it still missed new variations and unfamiliar image types. Still, YOLO was fast, and with a bit of post-processing rules (and some human correction), it was actually practical. So, I built a website. Upload an image → YOLO model counts microgels and cells Human-in-the-loop → check results, draw or delete boxes if needed Get accurate counts of only the microgels/cells you want Export results directly to Excel Plus: export YOLO training .txt labels → quickly refine datasets for future training In short, I now had a pipeline to get labeling done much faster and generate usable datasets for improving the model. And yes… I built the whole website in a single day. 😎 Here’s my GitHub if you want to try it yourself: Frontend Backend I also deployed the website! It’s a bit slow (since I don’t have any lab funding 😅), but it works pretty well using Hugging Face for the server and Netlify for the frontend: 👉 Live Demo
